claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen or fryer confirmed. The menu is naturally low in wheat due to its macrobiotic, rice-based focus, but cross-contamination from shared surfaces or utensils cannot be ruled out.

Standard soy sauce (which contains wheat) is likely used in seasoning, as no tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere in available sources. Celiac diners must ask specifically about soy sauce used in cooking.
The café philosophy is fully plant-based — no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy are used in the main kitchen — so vegan cross-contact is very unlikely in normal operation.

Staff are trained macrobiotic practitioners knowledgeable about ingredients sourced from the adjacent natural foods store; however, no formal allergy protocol or allergen-menu documentation has been confirmed.
All standard desserts are made without eggs, dairy, or refined sugar; soy-milk soft-serve is used throughout the sweets menu.
The daily lunch uses organic, pesticide-free vegetables and whole grains (enzyme brown rice); no animal products appear in the main menu.
No dedicated GF kitchen or fryer confirmed. Baked goods (cheesecake, cream puffs, toast) are prepared in the same small café space as all beverages; cross-contamination cannot be ruled out.
The egg sandwich filling uses wasabi mayonnaise with dashi flavoring; standard Japanese dashi may include wheat-containing soy sauce. No GF soy sauce alternative is documented.
Milk and dairy products are used throughout the menu (lattes, cheesecake, butter toast, cream puffs); plant-milk alternatives are not confirmed available.

No published allergy policy or staff allergy-handling protocol found. Reservations are accepted by phone (052-746-9134), which is the recommended channel to ask about specific dietary needs before visiting.
Plain black drip coffee and straight espresso are naturally free of gluten, dairy, and animal products — a safe baseline for both celiac and vegan diners.

Tonkatsu (breaded pork cutlet) and kara-age (fried chicken) are core menu items; both are wheat-breaded or wheat-battered, and no dedicated fryer for gluten-free items has been reported. Shared-fryer cross-contamination is the expected default.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (含む小麦) is the assumed condiment throughout the menu; no tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative has been mentioned by any source.
All set meals include meat or seafood as the protein; kitchen surfaces and cookware are shared. No vegan-only preparation zone or protocol has been mentioned anywhere.

No allergy handling protocol has been documented by any reviewer or the restaurant itself. This is a small family-run kitchen; allergen queries would need to be made in Japanese directly with the family.

Family-run kitchen with direct communication possible; a Japanese-speaking diner can speak face-to-face with the people actually cooking the food, which is preferable to large chain restaurants where kitchen staff may be untrained on allergy protocols.

name: レストラン ペルージュ (Restaurant Perouges)

claims.text: House-baked bread is served as part of the meal, meaning wheat flour is actively used in the kitchen. Flour-thickened sauces are standard in classical French cooking. No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or protocol is mentioned.
This is a French kitchen; soy sauce is not a listed ingredient. However, no explicit confirmation that soy sauce or wheat-based condiments are absent from all preparations.
Animal proteins (pigeon, veal, foie gras, rabbit, wild game) are central to the menu. Complete separation from vegan dishes is not possible in this kitchen.
Tabelog listing explicitly states: 苦手な食材、アレルギー等はご予約時にお伝えください。当日ですと対応しかねる場合がございます。（Please inform us of food dislikes and allergies at time of reservation; same-day requests may not be accommodable.）
All stocks and sauces made in-house from scratch by the chef, giving the kitchen full control over ingredients — facilitating custom preparation when notified in advance.
80–90% of vegetables used are certified organic or pesticide-free, sourced directly from named farms; antibiotic-free meats and wild-caught seafood used throughout.

name: ルーキーズこだわり生パスタ。時々ふんわりパンケーキ。 (Rookies Kodawari Nama Pasta. Tokidoki Funwar)

claims.text: 生パスタが主力商品であり、厨房内に小麦粉が常時大量に存在する環境。グルテンフリー対応に関する情報はどのソースにも記載がなく、交差汚染リスクは高いと推定される。
乳製品・卵を使った料理が主力で、ヴィーガン向けメニューの設定はなく、動物性食材との接触を回避する体制の記載は確認されていない。
No information available on cross-contamination controls. The kitchen is a small counter operation and no allergen protocols are documented.
Standard wheat-brewed shoyu is the defining ingredient of the ramen. No wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned in any source.
All broth is animal-based (chicken and/or pork bone); no plant-only preparation exists at this shop.

name: 柳城 NAGOYA CASTLE (Ryujo Nagoya Castle)

claims.text: No information about cross-contamination controls is publicly documented. Standard Cantonese kitchen workflows involve shared woks, utensils, and prep surfaces with wheat-containing ingredients throughout service.
Wheat-containing soy sauce is a foundational ingredient in Cantonese cooking and used throughout the menu. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Lard is traditional in dim sum pastry, and oyster sauce and other animal-derived condiments are ubiquitous in Cantonese kitchens. No vegan cross-contact protocols are documented.

The hotel states that allergy accommodations require advance notice and may be declined if customer safety cannot be guaranteed; requests should be directed to the reservation desk (052-908-8930, 10:00–18:30).
Luxury hotel setting with dedicated reservation staff, making advance allergy communication more feasible than at a typical independent restaurant.

name: 彩膳中華　杏ズ (Saizen Chuka Anzu)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or cross-contamination protocols are documented in any available source. The kitchen prepares wheat-based noodles (the vegan dandan noodles use egg-free domestic wheat noodles) alongside adapted GF dishes.

The kitchen uses homemade soy sauce koji (醤油麹) as a core condiment. No source confirms wheat-free or tamari soy sauce is used. Standard soy sauce in Chinese cooking contains wheat; celiacs must ask explicitly whether a wheat-free alternative is available for their specific dishes.
Not a fully vegan restaurant — meat and seafood dishes are prepared in the same kitchen. No source documents whether dedicated cookware or utensils are used for vegan preparations.

Multiple reviewers confirm staff ask about dietary preferences and allergies at the table, and the owner-chef explains each dish personally — suggesting genuine attentiveness rather than a scripted allergy protocol.
No chemical seasonings (MSG) or refined white sugar used anywhere in the kitchen.
Staff proactively ask about dietary restrictions; the chef personally brings dishes to the table and explains every ingredient, enabling real-time dialogue about allergen concerns.
English menu clearly marks vegan options, reducing communication friction for non-Japanese-speaking diners with dietary needs.
